title: How has toxoplasma turned the world into zombies?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite whose life cycle completes in cats. They cover how it spreads (cat feces in soil, undercooked livestock, rodents), how it alters rodent behavior (attraction to cat urine, slowed reflexes that lead to being eaten by cats), and the research on human infection: reaction-time deficits, opposite personality shifts in men and women, dopamine and testosterone links per Dr. Jaroslav Flegr of Charles University in Prague, a car-accident study, and a possible link to schizophrenia and nitric oxide. They plug the Animal Planet show Monsters Inside Me and close with a listener mail story from Bonnie of Boulder, Colorado.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Toxoplasma
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter, then introduce Toxoplasma gondii as a zoonotic parasite tied to a new Animal Planet show, Monsters Inside Me, and note its complex life cycle that ends in cats.

segments.title: Prevalence and transmission
segments.summary: Toxoplasma infects an estimated up to eight percent of the world population, with large country differences (Brazil sixty-seven percent, UK seven percent). Transmission occurs through cat feces, especially mixed with soil, and undercooked livestock. Pregnant women are warned to avoid cleaning cat litter.

segments.title: Life cycle and rodent intermediate host
segments.summary: The parasite spreads from soil into rodents, travels through the bloodstream to the brain, and completes its life cycle when infected rodents are eaten by cats.

segments.title: Behavioral changes in infected rodents
segments.summary: Infected rats lose their fear of cat urine, are drawn to cat-urine-soaked bedding, and have slowed motor reflexes, which makes them easier for cats to catch. Other innate fears remain intact.

segments.title: Effects on humans and Dr. Flegr's research
segments.summary: Human latent infection was long thought harmless, but studies found slower reaction times in infected people. Dr. Jaroslav Flegr of Charles University in Prague reports personality differences by gender and suggests dopamine and testosterone as likely mechanisms, while stressing correlation rather than causation.

segments.title: Car accidents, schizophrenia and nitric oxide
segments.summary: A 2002 Prague driving study linked infection to a higher risk of car accidents. The hosts also mention a correlation between toxoplasmosis and schizophrenia, nitric oxide levels, and cat ownership, citing Stanley Medical Research Center research. They discuss whether the findings are overstated.

segments.title: Monsters Inside Me plug and site promotion
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the Animal Planet show Monsters Inside Me, airing Wednesdays at nine, and its website, and thank Robert Lamb for research pointers.

segments.title: Listener mail: Bonnie of Boulder
segments.summary: Bonnie writes that after listening to a hypermiling podcast she drove slowly and avoided a head-on collision with a wrong-way driver on a rainy highway. The hosts joke about a key to the city and T-shirt ideas.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminder to send listener stories and T-shirt ideas to the show email, and a pointer to HowStuffWorks.
